stem: A mother with a 2 year-old boy presents to the emergency department with a six-hour history of episodic excessive crying. He looks unwell and is tachycardic. On physical examination. he passed some blood with mucus per rectum. Ultrasound shows a “target sign”. What is the most likely diagnosis for the above given scenario?
expl: Toddler with episodic crying (colic), blood and mucus per rectum (red currant jelly) and an ultrasound target sign = intussusception.

why.A: Perforation gives peritonitis and free air, not a target sign.
why.B: Correct.
why.C: A polyp bleeds painlessly, without colic or a target sign.
why.D: Meckel's bleeds painlessly (or acts as a lead point) — the target sign means intussusception.

stem: A 1-month-old infant presents with bilious vomiting, irritability, and hemodynamic instability. Abdominal X-ray shows multiple air-fluid levels and absent rectal gas, suggesting high intestinal obstruction. What is the most appropriate next imaging study?
expl: Bilious vomiting in an infant = malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise; the imaging gold standard is an upper GI contrast study. (The slide warns it takes time — a child with frank ischaemia/shock goes straight to laparotomy, but that isn't offered here.)

why.A: Ultrasound (SMA/SMV) is operator-dependent and not the gold standard.
why.B: Correct.
why.C: CT is generally avoided in neonates and infants.
why.D: Waiting risks losing the whole midgut.

stem: A 4-week-old infant presents with non-bilious, projectile vomiting after every feed. The baby appears hungry between episodes and has mild dehydration. What is the best initial imaging study?
expl: Projectile non-bilious vomiting at 4 weeks in a hungry, dehydrated baby = pyloric stenosis → ultrasound (thick, elongated pyloric muscle) is the gold standard.

why.B: Upper GI series works but uses radiation and is second line.
why.C: Correct.
why.D: Not used in infants for this.

stem: A one-day-old neonate has not passed meconium (Hirschsprung disease suspected). How do you investigate?
ansText: Contrast enema first — it shows the narrow aganglionic segment and transition zone (the source's recall answer was "barium enema"). Diagnosis is confirmed by rectal suction biopsy (gold standard: absent ganglion cells). Rectal manometry shows an absent recto-anal inhibitory reflex.

stem: infant presents with bilious vomiting that started within the first 24 hours of life. The infant has not passed meconium and has shown signs of abdominal distension?

opts.t: Intestinal obstruction due to Hirschsprung disease

srcNote: Only three answer choices are supplied in the source.
expl: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with midgut volvulus until proven otherwise — the emergency to exclude first. Missing meconium in the first 24 h isn't yet diagnostic; Hirschsprung becomes likely when meconium is delayed beyond 24–48 h with distension.

why.A: Possible, but the bilious vomiting must be treated as volvulus until an upper GI study excludes it.
why.B: Correct.
why.C: Pyloric stenosis presents at 2–8 weeks with NON-bilious vomiting.

stem: one-year-old child was brought to ER due to abdominal for 24h. mother noticed the pain to be intermittent and associated with hip flexion. Later, the child developed abdominal distention and passed a red currant jelly stool. Physical examination revealed a palpable mass at the right upper quadrant. Ultrasound showed a target sign (doughnut sign) at the right upper quadrant. Which of the following is appropriate initial management?
srcNote: c (Common Pediatric Surgical Emergencies) Other source key (Final 439 F Q12): The source uses air reduction: A. Air enema A
expl: Classic intussusception (colicky pain, red currant jelly stool, RUQ mass, target sign) in a child without peritonitis or shock → resuscitate, then therapeutic (contrast/air) enema reduction — first line.

why.A: Observation lets the bowel become ischaemic.
why.B: Surgery only if the enema fails or there is peritonitis, perforation or shock.
why.C: Correct.

stem: Patient was diagnosed with Pyloric stenosis , what is the best management?
expl: Pyloric stenosis → resuscitate and correct the hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, then pyloromyotomy (split the muscle down to intact mucosa).

why.B: Endoscopic dilation isn't the treatment.
why.C: It won't resolve with medical management.
why.D: NG decompression is part of resuscitation, not the treatment.

stem: A case of infant who is suffering from signs of bowel obstruction, failure to eat, and deteriorating. And asking about the location of the cecum , x ray enlarged gas bubble with absence of gas in bowel?
srcNote: (Common pediatric surgical problems??) Abbreviated source recall; clinical details are incomplete.
expl: In malrotation the caecum doesn't reach the RLQ — it lies high in the right upper quadrant/epigastrium, with Ladd's bands crossing the duodenum (hence the big gastric bubble and gasless distal bowel).

why.B: The colon may end up left-sided in non-rotation, but the classic malrotated caecum lies in the RUQ.
why.C: That's the normal position.

stem: 3-month-old baby presented with a picture of Malrotation, what is your management?
srcNote: (Common pediatric surgical problems) The source refers to a picture, but no associated image is supplied.
expl: Malrotation is treated with Ladd's procedure; the slides teach it by laparotomy (open), the standard especially when volvulus is possible.

why.B: Laparoscopic Ladd's is used in selected stable children, but the lecture's answer is laparotomy.
why.C: Endoscopy has no role.
why.D: CT isn't treatment and is avoided in infants.

stem: A case of a patient presenting to the EM with signs and symptoms of left testicular torsion, what is the best mx for this pt ?
expl: After detorsion, both testes are fixed — the bell-clapper anomaly that allowed torsion is usually bilateral, so the opposite testis is at risk.

why.B: Leaves the contralateral testis at risk.
why.C: Fixing only the normal side ignores the torsed testis.

stem: Eighteen-month-old baby presented to emergency department with six hours history of episodic excessive crying and pulling legs up. His heart rate was 140 b/m and blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg. On physical examination, a mass was felt at his upper abdomen. What is the best imaging modality to reach the diagnosis in this boy?
expl: Toddler with colicky crying, legs drawn up and an abdominal mass = intussusception → ultrasound (target/doughnut sign) is the gold standard.

why.B: CT adds radiation and isn't needed.
why.C: Correct.
why.D: Upper GI series is for malrotation.

stem: An 18 months old healthy boy presents to the emergency department by his mother with a six- hour history of vomiting and, episodic excessive crying and pulling legs up. Mother said her child had an URTI 1 week ago. He looks agitated and is tachycardic. On physical examination, a mass is felt at his lower abdomen and rectal examination revealed a blood with mucus per rectum. What is the most common site for this disease?
expl: Idiopathic childhood intussusception (Peyer's patch hypertrophy after a viral illness) is almost always ileocolic — the ileum telescopes into the caecum.

why.B: Colo-colic is rare.
why.C: Ileo-ileal is less common (often post-operative or with a lead point).

stem: In testicular torsion, What is the Ischemia time till the injury becomes irreversible?
expl: Testicular salvage is high if detorsed within about 6 hours and falls steeply after that; by 12–24 h the testis is usually lost — the irreversible window is 6–12 h.

why.B: Correct.
why.C: Most testes are already lost by then.

stem: A two-year-old healthy boy presented to emergency department with one hour history of choking and his face went blue for few seconds. Subsequently, he developed a noisy breathing. On physical examination, he had a stridor and his oxygen saturation was 98% in room air. His chest examination revealed decreased air entry on the right side and wheezing sounds. His chest X-RAY showed hyperinflation of the right lung. What is the most appropriate intervention for this boy?
expl: Choking episode then stridor/wheeze, decreased air entry and unilateral hyperinflation (ball-valve) = inhaled foreign body → bronchoscopy (rigid) to remove it.

why.A: Bronchodilators don't remove a foreign body.
why.B: Physiotherapy can dislodge it into the airway — dangerous.
why.C: Correct.

stem: A three-week-old baby boy presented to emergency department with progressive abdominal distention of two weeks duration and he required anal stimulation for passage of bowel motions. His abdomen was distended and rectal examination was explosive of gas and foul-smelling feces. His abdominal x-ray showed dilated bowel loops with no air in rectum. What is the most likely diagnosis in the above given Scenario?
expl: Infant with progressive distension, needing stimulation to pass stool, explosive gas and foul stool on rectal exam, no rectal air = Hirschsprung disease (± enterocolitis).

why.B: Functional constipation doesn't cause distension from 1 week of age with explosive decompression.
why.C: Anal atresia is seen at birth on inspection.
why.D: Meconium plug clears after the first passage and doesn't cause weeks of distension.

stem: A 10-year-old girl presents with fever, vomiting and significant right lower quadrant abdominal pain for 2 days. Her examination reveals rebound tenderness in the night lower quadrant. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Fever, vomiting and RLQ pain with rebound tenderness in a 10-year-old = acute appendicitis (peak 10–12 years).

why.A: Meckel's diverticulitis is far less common.
why.B: Ovarian torsion is sudden severe pain, often without fever.
why.C: UTI doesn't cause RLQ rebound; urinalysis excludes it.

stem: A 12-year-old girl presented to ER with a history of swallowing small metallic toy 6 hours back. She is currently asymptomatic. Investigation confirmed the presence of FB in the stomach. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management?

opts.t: Urgent upper GI endoscopy for FB retrieval.

srcNote: The interval unit after "2-3" in choice C is missing from the source.
expl: A small blunt foreign body that has reached the stomach in an asymptomatic child will usually pass → observe with serial X-rays. Urgent removal is for oesophageal button batteries, multiple magnets, sharp objects or symptoms.

why.A: Not needed for a small blunt object in the stomach.
why.B: Far too invasive.
why.C: Correct.

stem: 3 years old girl, presented to clinic with Hx of constipation. The most important features may point to termed surgical cause?

opts.t: delay passing of mecanime > 48 hours after birth.

srcNote: ? This question seems missing some info or the age is wrong Encopresis isn't looked at before 4 years. The source marks its answer as uncertain; the original key is retained.
expl: Constipation from birth with delayed passage of meconium (beyond the first 24–48 h) points to an organic, surgical cause — Hirschsprung disease.

why.B: A short history suggests functional constipation.
why.C: Soiling (encopresis) is typical of functional constipation with overflow.

stem: 6 week baby, presented with recurrent progressing projectile nonbilious vomiting. They told the mother that he has GERD and they give him ranitidine. There was No improvement , she came back after 1 week with her child having recurrent vomiting and severe dehydration. Normal abdominal examination. X-ray: unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis for this baby?
expl: Projectile non-bilious vomiting at 6 weeks, worsening despite anti-reflux treatment, with dehydration = pyloric stenosis (the X-ray is often unremarkable).

why.B: GERD doesn't cause progressive projectile vomiting with dehydration.
why.C: Hirschsprung causes distension and delayed stool, with bilious vomiting.

stem: A 12 years old girl had appendectomy for perforated appendicitis. Which of the following is the commonest long-term complication?
expl: The commonest long-term complication after appendectomy (especially perforated) is adhesive small-bowel obstruction. Infertility risk from perforated appendicitis in girls is debated and less common.

why.B: Not related.
why.C: Not related.

stem: A 9-month-old baby boy, presented to the emergency department with a persistent cough, stridor and cyanosis started suddenly 1 hour back while he was eating peanuts. Which of the following is the most appropriate first step in his management?

opts.t: Confirm the presence of foreign body by performing urgent bronchoscopy
Give him ventolin nebulizer as soon as possible

expl: Stridor and cyanosis = an airway emergency → secure the airway first (ABC); bronchoscopy follows once the child is stable.

why.B: Bronchoscopy comes after the airway is secured.
why.C: Never delay for history in a cyanosed child.
why.D: Nebulizers don't treat a foreign body.

stem: A 10-year-old boy who was healthy presented to the ER with 24 right lower quadrant pain associated with fever and vomiting. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness in the right lower quadrant with guarding. His temperature was 38.5 C White blood cell count was elevated and urine was clear. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in his management?

opts.t: Confirm the diagnosis by performing U/S abdomen
Confirm the diagnosis by performing CT abdomen

srcNote: The related 428 recall has an unclear requirement and conflicting source keys; its choices and key are preserved below. Other source key (Final 428 Q14 (p. 302)): A child presented to the ER with right iliac fossa pain for 24 hours with nausea vomiting : A. Do CT scan B. Do US C. Admit him for appendectomy D. Antibiotic and discharge C, QUESTION REQUIREMENT IS NOT CLEAR, B
expl: Even with a classic picture, the doctor wants an ultrasound before appendectomy (fast, no radiation, excludes mimics) — the slide says imaging isn't always needed, but follow the lecture and this key.

why.B: CT only if US is inconclusive — radiation in a child.
why.C: Observation delays treatment and risks perforation.
why.D: The step after the US confirms it.

stem: A young boy presented to the accident and emergency at 2:00 am with sudden onset of scrotal pain associated with scrotal swelling nausea and vomiting. Physical examination revealed an absent cremasteric reflex on the right hemiscrotum with a very tender right testicle lying in the horizontal plane. Urinalysis was negative. What will be the next step in the management?
expl: Sudden scrotal pain with vomiting, absent cremasteric reflex and a high horizontal tender testis = torsion → immediate scrotal exploration; imaging must not delay it.

why.B: Not treatment.
why.C: Ultrasound wastes time when the diagnosis is clinical.

stem: A 10 years old child presented with RLQ pain, fever, tenderness and guarding ,, with elevated WBC,, what is the next step in management?

opts.t: Give the patient fluids and monitor

expl: A child with clinically obvious appendicitis (RLQ pain, fever, guarding, high WBC) → urgent appendectomy.

why.B: Observation risks perforation (higher in children).
why.C: Antibiotics alone aren't standard for clear appendicitis with guarding.

stem: Child presented to the ER with a history of aspirating a peanut, had a stridor, dyspnea and cyanosis. what is the initial step in management:

opts.t: Confirm the diagnosis with rigid bronchoscope

expl: Stridor, dyspnoea and cyanosis after aspiration → secure the airway first, then remove the foreign body by rigid bronchoscopy.

why.A: Bronchoscopy comes once the airway is secure.
why.B: Correct.
why.C: Adrenaline is for anaphylaxis, not a foreign body.
why.D: A surgical airway is the last resort if the airway can't be secured otherwise.

stem: A 12 y/o girl post appendectomy after perforated appendix presented with pus in the pelvis, what is the most common known complication?
expl: After appendectomy for perforation (pelvic pus), the commonest known long-term complication is adhesions → adhesive small-bowel obstruction.

why.B: Infertility risk is debated and much less common.
why.C: Not a recognized complication.
